title: Atomic structure, isotopes and ions
blurb: Count the protons, neutrons and electrons in any atom or ion, and tell isotopes from ions at a glance.
question: A lab handout lists sulfur-34 as 'atomic number 16' and asks for the number of neutrons, then asks how the sulfide ion S²⁻ differs from a neutral sulfur atom. How do you work out both answers?

teach.body: Formally, an atom is the smallest unit of an element, made of a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in energy levels (shells). In plain English: a tiny, heavy, positive core with a huge, almost weightless cloud of negative electrons around it. The nucleus holds nearly all of the mass; the electron cloud takes up nearly all of the volume.

teach.caption: Protons and neutrons have nearly equal mass. An electron's mass is negligible by comparison.

teach.body: The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons. It defines the element: every atom with 6 protons is carbon, and changing the proton count changes the element. The mass number (A) is protons plus neutrons, so neutrons = A − Z. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons, because the charges must cancel.

teach.caption: The number after the name (carbon-14) is always the mass number, never the atomic number.
Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties, because chemistry depends on electrons, not neutrons.

root.label: Ion: charged atom
root.sub: Electrons gained or lost; protons never change in reactions

teach.caption: Losing negative electrons leaves the atom positive. Gaining them makes it negative.

teach.body: Jordan, a pre-nursing student, is reviewing potassium for her HESI A2: atomic number 19, most common isotope potassium-39, and the K⁺ ion found in body fluids. Protons = 19. Neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20. A neutral atom has 19 electrons; K⁺ has lost one, so it has 18 electrons. Its mass number stays 39, because electrons add almost no mass.

teach.caption: Some isotopes have unstable nuclei that decay, giving off alpha, beta or gamma radiation. Each half-life halves what is left.

steps.label: Rutherford
steps.sub: Gold foil: small, dense, positive nucleus

teach.caption: Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. The average atomic mass on the periodic table is a weighted average of an element's isotopes, so it is a decimal.

teach.text: Isotopes differ in NEUTRONS; ions differ in ELECTRONS. Neither changes the proton count. And the atomic number is protons only: protons plus neutrons is the mass number. A cation LOST electrons (it did not gain protons).

items: Proton +1 and neutron 0 (both about 1 amu) sit in the nucleus; electron −1 (negligible mass) sits in shells.
Atomic number = protons and defines the element. Mass number = protons + neutrons.
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Neutral atom: electrons = protons.
Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons. Ions: same protons, different electrons.
Cation = lost electrons (+); anion = gained electrons (−).

summary: You can now find the protons, neutrons and electrons in any atom or ion from its atomic and mass numbers. You can also tell an isotope from an ion, explain why atomic masses are decimals and track a radioactive sample through its half-lives.

A.q: An atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. What is its mass number?

whyNot.0: 17 is the atomic number (protons only), not the mass number.
whyNot.1: 18 is the number of neutrons alone.
whyNot.3: 34 doubles the proton count; the mass number adds the actual neutrons (18), not a second 17.

A.q: Which quantity identifies an atom as a particular element?
A.why: The atomic number, the number of protons, defines the element. Change the protons and you have a different element.

whyNot.0: Atoms of one element can have different numbers of neutrons (isotopes) and remain that element.
whyNot.1: Electrons can be gained or lost to form ions without changing the element.
whyNot.2: Isotopes of the same element have different mass numbers, so it cannot define the element.

A.q: How do the isotopes carbon-12 and carbon-14 differ?
A.why: Both have 6 protons (both are carbon). Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8, a difference of two neutrons.

whyNot.0: Two more protons would make it a different element (oxygen), not carbon.
whyNot.2: Gaining electrons makes an ion, not an isotope; neutral isotopes have equal electrons.
whyNot.3: Isotopes are neutral atoms; a charge comes from losing electrons, which is an ion.

B.q: Magnesium has atomic number 12. How many electrons does a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺, have?
B.why: A neutral Mg atom has 12 electrons. The 2+ charge means it lost two, leaving 12 − 2 = 10.

whyNot.1: 12 is the electron count of the neutral atom, before it lost two electrons.
whyNot.2: 14 adds two electrons; a positive ion has lost electrons, not gained them.
whyNot.3: 24 is magnesium's approximate mass number (protons + neutrons), not its electrons.

B.q: Which statement about the atomic nucleus is correct?
options: It fills most of the volume of the atom
It has an overall negative charge
It holds nearly all of the atom's mass
B.why: Protons and neutrons (about 1 amu each) sit in the nucleus, so it holds nearly all of the mass while being tiny.

whyNot.0: The electron cloud takes up nearly all of the volume; the nucleus is tiny.
whyNot.1: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons; electrons are in shells around it.
whyNot.2: With protons (+) and neutral neutrons, the nucleus is positive.

B.q: A chlorine atom (17 protons) gains one electron. What does it become?
B.why: Gaining a negative electron gives 17 + 1 = 18 electrons and a 1− charge: the anion Cl⁻.

whyNot.0: A cation is positive, formed by losing electrons; gaining one makes the atom negative.
whyNot.2: 16 electrons would mean it lost one, which would make it positive.
whyNot.3: Changing electrons makes an ion; an isotope differs in neutrons.

C.q: A sulfide ion, S²⁻, comes from sulfur-32 (atomic number 16). Which particle count is correct?
C.why: Protons = 16 (atomic number). Neutrons = 32 − 16 = 16. The 2− charge means two electrons gained: 16 + 2 = 18.

whyNot.0: 14 electrons would be a 2+ ion; a 2− charge means electrons were gained.
whyNot.1: Protons never change when an ion forms; sulfur keeps 16.
whyNot.3: Neutrons = 32 − 16 = 16; the charge does not change the neutron count.

C.q: A tracer isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. A patient receives 40 mg. How much of the isotope remains undecayed after 18 hours?

whyNot.0: 10 mg is what remains after two half-lives (12 hours), not three.
whyNot.2: 13.3 mg divides by 3; each half-life halves the amount rather than removing a third.
whyNot.3: 20 mg is the amount after one half-life (6 hours).

C.q: Which pairing of scientist and contribution is correct?
C.why: Bohr placed electrons in fixed energy levels (orbits) around the nucleus.

whyNot.0: Thomson discovered the electron; the nucleus came from Rutherford's gold foil experiment.
whyNot.1: Rutherford discovered the nucleus; Thomson discovered the electron.
whyNot.3: The plum pudding model is Thomson's; Dalton proposed a solid, indivisible sphere.

reteach.title: ID badge, backpack and jacket
reteach.question: Picture a student on campus with an ID badge, a backpack and a jacket. What changes who they are, what changes their weight, and what changes their 'charge'?

blocks.body: Protons are the ID badge: swap it and you are a different person (a different element). Neutrons are the backpack: add or remove books and you weigh more or less (a different isotope), but you are still you. Electrons are the jacket: take it off or put on an extra one and you look different (an ion with a charge), yet your badge and weight barely change.

blocks.text: Electrons are the only particle that changes in an ordinary chemical reaction. If a question says the protons changed, you are no longer looking at the same element.

explain.body: Protons (+1) and neutrons (0) each have a mass of about 1 amu and sit in the nucleus. Electrons (−1) are about 1/1836 amu and occupy shells around it. So the nucleus is tiny but heavy, and the cloud is huge but almost massless.

test.q: Which two particles have nearly the same mass?
test.why: Protons and neutrons are each about 1 amu; an electron is about 1/1836 of that.

whyNot.1: A proton is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron.
whyNot.2: A neutron is about 1 amu; an electron's mass is negligible.
whyNot.3: The electron is far lighter than the other two, so the three do not share a mass.

explain.body: Atomic number (Z) = protons, and it defines the element. Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. Neutrons = A − Z. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons.

test.q: Iron has atomic number 26. How many neutrons are in an atom of iron-56?

whyNot.0: 26 is the number of protons (the atomic number).
whyNot.2: 56 is the mass number: protons and neutrons together.
whyNot.3: 82 adds the two numbers; neutrons come from subtracting Z from A.

explain.body: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same protons) with different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers. Hydrogen has three: protium, deuterium and tritium. Isotopes share chemical properties. Some are radioactive and decay with a fixed half-life.

test.q: Protium, deuterium and tritium are isotopes of hydrogen. What do they have in common?
test.why: Isotopes of one element always share the proton count (here, 1 proton each).

whyNot.0: Neutrons are exactly what differ between isotopes (0, 1 and 2 here).
whyNot.1: Different neutron counts give different mass numbers (1, 2 and 3).
whyNot.3: Extra neutrons make each isotope heavier, so their masses differ.

explain.body: An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons. Metals tend to lose electrons, forming positive cations (Na⁺, Ca²⁺). Nonmetals tend to gain them, forming negative anions (Cl⁻, O²⁻). Protons never change.

test.q: A calcium atom (atomic number 20) becomes Ca²⁺. What happened to it?
test.why: Losing two negative electrons leaves 20 protons and 18 electrons: a 2+ cation.

whyNot.0: Gaining electrons would give a negative charge (2−).
whyNot.1: Protons do not change when ions form; 22 protons would be titanium.
whyNot.2: Losing protons would change the element (to argon) and could not create a positive charge.
